extracted.intended_audience: children's book writers and illustrators, SCBWI members, and the children's publishing community
extracted.subtask_description: Implicit and explicit evaluative signals drawn from the SCBWI Golden Kite Awards announcement describing what the various award committees rewarded across categories (humor, nonfiction for different ages, picture book text and illustration, middle-grade, illustrated older-readers, YA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sid Fleischman Humor Award (humor writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition for outstanding humor in children's writing (the annual Sid Fleischman Humor Award).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award highlights books with strong comic voice and effective humor for young readers; example winner: Tracy Badua’s Freddie vs. the Family Curse. (No formal scoring guidance given on page.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfiction Text for Younger Readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Award recognizing excellence in nonfiction books aimed at younger readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee chair Tiffany Jewell described Our Planet as a book “that will be used in classrooms across the country,” indicating the committee values classroom usability and educational applicability in younger-reader nonfiction. Example winner: Our Planet: There’s No Place Like Earth (illustrated by David Litchfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonfiction Text for Older Readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Award recognizing nonfiction aimed at older children/teens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners show imaginative approaches to nonfiction voice and subject matter; e.g., Stacy McAnulty’s Save the People! Halting Human Extinction (honor) and Tara Lazar’s Absurd Words (winner) demonstrate use of distinctive narrative voice and humor/engagement appropriate to older readers. Page notes McAnulty composed two manuscripts together, imagining “Earth telling her story,” suggesting narrative perspective and voice are meaningful factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle Grade Fiction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is competitive (committee rated ~170 books). Judges appear to value authentic voice, lived-experience grounding, and the handling of identity and historical subject matter — example winner Michael Leali’s The Civil War of Amos Abernathy, described as based on his experiences as a historical re-enactor, a homeschooled child, and a young queer person whose identity becomes a celebration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture Book Text
rubrics_metrics.description: Award for excellence in picture book writing (text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee praised Fly’s “poetic language [that] captures the rhythms of childhood play,” indicating a premium on lyrical/poetic language that authentically evokes childhood experience and play rhythms. Example winner: Fly by Brittany J. Thurman (illustrated by Anna Cunha).

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture Book Illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: Award for excellence in picture book illustration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges value illustration style and emotional/visual impact; committee chair Shadra Strickland called Kumo the Bashful Cloud “beautifully impressionistic—it would make anyone want to look up,” indicating preference for evocative, impressionistic art that elicits wonder. Example winner: Nathalie Dion for Kumo the Bashful Cloud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrated Book for Older Readers (author-illustrator integration and originality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Award for illustrated books intended for older readers, often where text and art are tightly integrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners may demonstrate originality in visual narrative and inventive development of concept (example: Isabel Roxas’s The Adventures of Team Pom: Squid Happens began as a single painting, became a picture book, then a self-published series and finally a picked-up book), suggesting judges reward creative visual storytelling and originality in format/approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Young Adult Fiction (historical/social resonance and emotional depth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Award for outstanding young adult fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges appear to value historical authenticity, cultural representation, emotional resonance, and social relevance. Example winner Emily Inouye Huey’s Beneath the Wide Silk Sky is a World War II–era story of a young Japanese American photographer; the author ties the work to experiences teaching in a detention center and family history of imprisonment, signaling weight given to subject matter with historical and social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitiveness and committee deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection process involves committees reviewing many entries and close deliberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Middle Grade Fiction committee rated some 170 books; Shadra Strickland said, “I can tell you there were almost fights in trying to pick” the winners. This implies rigorous comparative judgment, close debate among judges, and high standards rather than formulaic scoring.
